strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: predictive world models for mobile GUI agents, where visual state changes can matter for long-horizon planning.

The core idea of Symbolic Text Representation is practical and well motivated: replacing text with placeholders lets the diffusion model focus on GUI layout/graphics while an LLM handles text generation.
The paper presents a coherent end-to-end system, including STR prediction, GUI-text prediction, and an action-selection loop for improving app agents.

Experiments cover multiple evaluation angles: visual GUI quality, trajectory synthesis, agent step accuracy, comparisons to language and vision world-model baselines, and ablations on static text preservation and action instructions.
Qualitative examples and failure cases are useful and make the strengths and limitations of the approach relatively easy to understand.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not fully convincing for a top-tier acceptance. The main sampled test evaluation uses only 57 episodes, and many metrics rely on LLM-as-judge prompts, which raises concerns about variance, bias, and calibration.

The agent improvement is modest in absolute terms: for example, T3A improves from 43.13 to 49.20 step accuracy and M3A from 46.01 to 50.16. This supports usefulness but not the stronger claims about robust long-horizon decision-making.

The method depends heavily on several brittle components: OCR quality, hand-designed text-symbol detection by color thresholds, LLM prompt reliability, heuristic text overlay, and generated GUI plausibility. Error propagation is not analyzed deeply.

Baselines are somewhat limited and may not be optimally adapted to this setting. In particular, comparisons to image-editing/UI generation models and text world models do not fully establish that ViMo is the best possible visual GUI world-model approach.

The paper evaluates mostly step-wise action accuracy and simulated trajectory agreement, not true closed-loop task success in real apps or emulators. This weakens the practical claim that the model improves real-world app-agent planning.

Generalization is only partially demonstrated. The train/validation/test splits involve the same 19 apps, and the novel-action examples are qualitative, so it remains unclear how well ViMo transfers to unseen apps, unseen UI styles, or genuinely out-of-distribution workflows.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a complex pipeline: the exact diffusion fine-tuning setup, LLM versions/settings, OCR configuration, data preprocessing, action-option generation, prompt sensitivity, and compute cost are not specified sufficiently in the main paper.

The novelty is meaningful but incremental: the system combines diffusion-based image editing, OCR/text masking, LLM text prediction, and LLM-based action selection. STR is a useful engineering idea, but the technical contribution is not especially deep.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: using visual world models to improve long-horizon mobile GUI agents, where purely textual state predictions can miss actionable visual details.

The STR decomposition is a sensible engineering idea for GUI generation: predict layout/graphics with placeholders and delegate text reconstruction to an LLM, avoiding common diffusion failures on small text.
The paper includes several comparison axes, including GUI quality, trajectory synthesis, agent step accuracy, and ablations for static text preservation and action-instruction conditioning.
Qualitative examples make the intended behavior of the model easy to understand.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not strong enough for the central claims. The main agent gains are small in absolute terms, evaluated mostly as step accuracy rather than real task success in an executable environment, and it is unclear whether the improvements translate to robust long-horizon completion.

Evaluation relies heavily on LLM-as-judge metrics for instructional accuracy, action readiness, trajectory matching, and action selection. This creates circularity because LLMs are also key components of the method, and the paper provides insufficient validation of judge reliability against human labels or real emulator outcomes.

The experimental protocol appears weak and potentially unrealistic: only a sampled subset of 57 episodes is used for several evaluations, train/test splits share the same 19 apps, and prompts mention action options from the dataset, raising concerns that the setting may be closer to reranking known candidate actions than autonomous planning.

Baselines are not fully convincing. Generic image-editing and GUI-generation baselines are likely poorly matched to next-GUI prediction, while language and HTML baselines are adapted in unclear ways. The paper does not establish that the comparisons are fair, well-tuned, or representative of the strongest alternatives.

The claimed novelty as the first visual GUI world model is overstated and insufficiently positioned relative to prior GUI generation, visual web/world models, emulator-based methods, and model-based planning for agents.

The method depends on several brittle handcrafted stages: OCR masking, LLM filtering of static text, color-threshold placeholder detection, LLM semantic role assignment, and heuristic text rendering. Failure modes are acknowledged but not systematically quantified.

Reproducibility is limited. Important implementation details are missing or vague, the project link is blank in the manuscript text, proprietary models such as GPT-4o appear to be used for data conversion and prediction, and compute/training details are not sufficiently specified.

The paper contains numerous clarity and polish issues, including typos, inconsistent names such as ViMo/VisMo and APP-Agnet/Langugae/Additioanl, malformed references, and some prompts with apparent output-format errors. These issues reduce confidence in the care taken with the work.

The generalization evidence is weak. Examples of novel action-GUI combinations are qualitative only, while the actual dataset is limited to 19 apps and same-app splits, leaving open whether the model works beyond memorized app layouts and transitions.

The practical value is unclear because the method may be slower and more expensive than directly querying a multimodal agent, given that it invokes image generation plus multiple LLM calls per candidate action without a careful latency/cost analysis.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: GUI world models for mobile app agents, where text-only future-state prediction loses actionable visual information.

The Symbolic Text Representation is a simple but effective design choice for separating GUI layout/graphics prediction from exact text rendering, directly addressing a real failure mode of diffusion-based GUI generation.
The evaluation covers both intrinsic GUI generation quality and downstream agent decision making, and compares against relevant language-based and vision-based world-model baselines.
Empirical results are consistently favorable: ViMo improves the harmonic GUI quality score, trajectory synthesis accuracy, and step-wise action prediction accuracy across several agents.
The ablations on preserving static text and using natural-language action instructions support the main design choices, and the appendix provides useful implementation prompts and additional results.
weaknesses: Several key metrics rely on LLM-as-judge evaluation, including instructional accuracy, action readiness, trajectory correctness, and action selection. This creates potential evaluator bias and makes the strength of the evidence less conclusive without human validation or calibration analysis.

The downstream improvements, while consistent, are modest in absolute terms: for example step accuracy improves from 46.01 to 50.16 for M3A and from 43.13 to 49.20 for T3A, leaving overall performance still low.

The evaluation is limited to 19 apps and a sampled test split of 57 episodes for some experiments. Although full-split GUI-quality results are included, broader app coverage and stronger generalization tests would make the claims more convincing.

The baselines are somewhat imperfect fits: HTML-vision, IP2P, and UI-diffuser are adapted to this setting, but it is unclear whether they are optimized as carefully as ViMo for mobile GUI future prediction.

The method depends on several brittle components: OCR quality, rectangle-symbol detection by color thresholds, LLM text prediction, and handcrafted text overlay. Failure cases are acknowledged, but the paper does not quantify how often each component fails.

The project link appears blank in the manuscript, and reproducibility details are incomplete for a top-tier submission, especially model sizes, training compute, fine-tuning settings, exact LLM versions, and release plans for data/code.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: enabling mobile app agents to reason over future GUI states in visual form rather than relying only on textual descriptions.

The Symbolic Text Representation is a sensible and practically motivated decomposition: diffusion handles GUI layout/graphics while an LLM handles text, directly targeting the well-known weakness of image generators on small GUI text.

The evaluation covers several relevant axes, including GUI generation quality, downstream step-wise action prediction, zero-shot app generalization, online AndroidWorld navigation, ablations, user studies, and qualitative examples.
Results are directionally consistent: ViMo generally outperforms visual baselines, language world models, and no-world-model agent variants, with useful gains in downstream agent accuracy.
The appendix provides useful implementation detail for text-symbol detection, prompting, dataset construction, additional world-model comparisons, randomness analysis, and inference cost.
weaknesses: The evidence is not fully convincing for a top-tier acceptance: many core metrics rely on LLM judges, and the proposed method itself uses GPT-4o for text prediction, action selection, data conversion, and evaluation, creating risk of evaluator bias and difficult-to-interpret gains.

The evaluation scale is relatively limited. The main GUI-quality evaluation uses a sampled subset of 57 episodes and the user study uses only 80 generated samples total, which is small for broad claims about real-world GUI world modeling.

Downstream improvements are modest in absolute terms: for example M3A improves from 46.01 to 50.16 step accuracy and online task accuracy from 33.19 to 40.95, while adding around two minutes of inference per request. The practical value is therefore less clear than the paper’s framing suggests.

Baselines are somewhat underdeveloped. Stronger or more carefully adapted multimodal prediction/planning baselines, OCR-assisted baselines, structured UI element prediction baselines, and modern GUI-agent planners would be needed to isolate the contribution of STR from prompting and LLM selection effects.

The method depends heavily on brittle heuristics for detecting generated text placeholders by color and rectangularity. The paper acknowledges failure cases, but does not quantify how often placeholder detection fails or how errors propagate through the agent pipeline.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the project link appears blank in the manuscript, release details are vague, and reliance on proprietary LLMs and user-commitment-gated checkpoints limits independent verification.

The claimed real-world applicability is weakened by latency and by the fact that generated GUIs may hallucinate impossible states. The paper does not sufficiently evaluate safety-critical mispredictions, cascading failures, or robustness under app updates and diverse device settings.

The social impact discussion is shallow; requiring a user commitment for checkpoint access is not a meaningful safeguard against misuse, especially for a model intended to simulate and guide GUI actions.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant problem: visual world models for mobile GUI agents, where textual-only future-state descriptions are insufficient for planning and pixel-based GUI generation struggles with readable text.

The proposed STR decomposition is intuitive and practically motivated: treating text boxes as symbolic placeholders and delegating content generation to an LLM addresses a real failure mode of diffusion-based GUI generation.
The paper includes several evaluation angles, including GUI quality, downstream step accuracy, zero-shot apps, online navigation, ablations, trajectory synthesis, and limited runtime analysis.
Qualitative examples make the core motivation easy to understand, especially the contrast between visually plausible GUI layout generation and distorted text rendering in image-only baselines.
weaknesses: The central contribution is technically rather incremental: it combines OCR-based text masking, an InstructPix2Pix-style diffusion model, heuristic rectangle detection, and LLM prompting. The paper does not provide a deep modeling advance beyond this pipeline, despite strong claims such as being the first visual GUI world model.

The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier venue. The main world-model evaluation uses only 57 sampled episodes, and the user study uses only 80 generated samples total, apparently 20 per method, which is too small for the breadth of claims made.

Many key metrics rely on LLM-as-judge evaluation, while GPT-4o is also used inside the method for text prediction, action conversion, filtering static text, and other pipeline steps. This creates potential circularity and bias, and the paper does not adequately validate the automatic judgments against independent ground truth.

The downstream gains are modest in absolute terms. For example, M3A improves from 46.01 to 50.16 step accuracy and T3A from 43.13 to 49.20. Some category-level results are weak or inconsistent, and the paper presents relative improvements in a way that overstates the practical magnitude.

Baselines are not fully satisfactory. Several world-model baselines are adapted by the authors, and the paper does not make clear that they are tuned comparably. Stronger alternatives such as structured UI-tree prediction, OCR/layout transfer baselines, or oracle/upper-bound variants are missing.

The method depends heavily on brittle heuristics: OCR quality, static text filtering by LLM, black-border/white-fill rectangle detection, and handcrafted text rendering. The paper itself shows failures where generated placeholders are not recognizable, but does not quantify how often these failures occur or how they affect downstream decisions.

There is no direct, rigorous evaluation of text correctness, layout-element correctness, or transition fidelity. Visual similarity, action readiness, and LLM judgment do not isolate whether the model predicts the actual next GUI state versus merely producing a plausible-looking screen.

The online evaluation is underdeveloped. It reports a single improvement on AndroidWorld but lacks statistical confidence, details about task selection, failure breakdowns, repeated runs, and comparison to stronger same-model baselines using equivalent prompting or extra compute.

Reproducibility is limited. The project link is blank in the manuscript, training hyperparameters and model sizes are underspecified, and checkpoint release is gated by an unspecified user commitment. This is problematic given the many pipeline components and LLM prompts involved.

The social-impact discussion is superficial. A visual GUI world model could enable automated manipulation, phishing-style UI simulation, or unsafe app interactions, but the paper only mentions a generic commitment requirement without concrete safeguards or evaluation of misuse risks.

The writing sometimes overclaims relative to the evidence, especially around real-world practicality. The reported inference can be around two minutes per request for three actions, which is substantial for interactive phone control, yet the paper frames deployment as lightweight and straightforward.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: app agents need predictive models of GUI state transitions for long-horizon planning, and text-only world models miss crucial visual/layout information.

The core idea of separating GUI graphics/layout generation from text rendering via Symbolic Text Representation is simple, well motivated, and practically useful for avoiding the known weakness of diffusion models on small UI text.
The paper provides a coherent system design: OCR-based STR construction, diffusion-based STR prediction, LLM-based GUI text prediction, and integration into action selection for existing app agents.

Empirical evaluation is broad relative to the problem setting, including GUI-generation quality, user study results, decision optimization with multiple app agents, comparisons to language and vision world models, zero-shot evaluation on unseen apps, online AndroidWorld evaluation, ablations, trajectory synthesis, and runtime analysis.
Results consistently support the main practical claim: ViMo improves downstream app-agent step/task accuracy over no world model and over several adapted world-model baselines.
The appendix includes useful implementation details and prompts, which improves reproducibility compared with many agent-system papers.
weaknesses: Novelty is solid but not exceptional. The method combines known components, including OCR masking, latent diffusion/image editing, and LLM-based text prediction; the main contribution is the task-specific integration rather than a fundamentally new modeling technique.

The evaluation relies heavily on LLM-based judgments for instructional accuracy, action readiness, and action selection, which may introduce evaluator bias and can overestimate functional correctness. Human evaluation helps, but covers only 80 samples and lacks detail on agreement, sampling, and participant quality control.

The decision-making gains, while consistent, are moderate in absolute terms: for example M3A improves from 46.01 to 50.16 step accuracy, and online T3A improves from 33.19 to 40.95 task accuracy. This is useful but not clearly transformative for app agents.

The test scale is somewhat limited for strong top-tier claims. The main sampled evaluation uses 57 episodes across 19 apps, and although additional full-split/randomness evidence is provided for generation metrics, downstream agent evaluations would benefit from larger and more statistically rigorous testing.

Comparisons to baselines are not fully satisfying. Several baselines are adapted or fine-tuned by the authors, and it is unclear whether they are optimized equally. Stronger comparisons to emulator-based planning, learned GUI-transition models, and recent multimodal agent planning systems would strengthen the paper.

The approach depends on several brittle heuristic stages, including OCR quality, static-text filtering, rectangle/color matching for text symbols, and handcrafted text overlay. The paper acknowledges some symbol-generation failures but does not deeply quantify how these errors propagate to agent decisions.

Reproducibility and accessibility are limited by reliance on proprietary LLMs such as GPT-4o/Gemini and by the proposed checkpoint access restriction. Exact training details, model sizes, compute, seeds, and release plan should be clearer for a top-tier submission.

The practical deployment story is mixed: ViMo adds roughly two minutes per request for three candidate actions, which may be too slow for many interactive mobile-agent settings despite the reported accuracy gains.

The safety discussion is rather shallow. A user commitment for checkpoint access is not a strong safeguard against misuse, and the paper could better address risks from GUI spoofing, automated manipulation, privacy leakage from screenshots, and agent actions in sensitive apps.
